Aspergillus fumigatus (Af) is a major mould pathogen found ubiquitously in the air. It commonly infects the airways of people with cystic fibrosis (CF) leading to Aspergillus bronchitis or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Resident alveolar macrophages and recruited neutrophils are important first lines of defence for clearance of Af in the lung. However, their contribution to the inflammatory phenotype in CF during Af infection is not well understood. Here, utilising CFTR deficient mice we describe a hyperinflammatory phenotype in both acute and allergic murine models of pulmonary aspergillosis. We show that during aspergillosis, CFTR deficiency leads to increased alveolar macrophage death and persistent inflammation of the airways in CF, accompanied by impaired fungal control. Utilising CFTR deficient murine cells and primary human CF cells we show that at a cellular level there is increased activation of NF{kappa}B and NFAT in response to Af which, as in in vivo models, is associated with increased cell death and reduced fungal control. Taken together, these studies indicate that CFTR deficiency promotes increased activation of inflammatory pathways, the induction of macrophage cell death and reduced fungal control contributing to the hyper-inflammatory of pulmonary aspergillosis phenotypes in CF.

Author SummaryThe airways of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) are commonly colonised with Aspergillus fumigatus (Af) resulting in a persistent hyperinflammatory state and the development of allergy. Understanding how first line defence innate cells, such as alveolar macrophages and neutrophils, contribute to this hyperinflammatory phenotype is important in developing novel treatments to preserve lung function in pwCF. In this study, we report that CFTR deficiency leads to increased alveolar macrophage death and persistent inflammation of the airways in pwCF, which is associated with impaired control of infection. We identify the increased activation of the transcription factors NF{kappa}B and NFAT as the mechanism of increased inflammatory cytokine production in CFTR deficient cells. This work is the first step in describing molecular mechanisms of hyperinflammation in CF in response to fungal infection and lays the groundwork for further dissection of inflammatory pathways to target with immunotherapeutic approaches.

Receptor crosstalk, the interaction between different receptors to modulate signaling, is crucial for fine-tuning the inflammatory responses of innate immune cells. Although the synergistic crosstalk between Toll-like receptor (TLR)4 and Fc gamma receptor (Fc{gamma}R) is well documented, the detailed mechanism underlying this synergy remains unclear. In this study, we addressed this knowledge gap by imaging the molecular organization of TLR4 and Fc{gamma}R on the macrophage cell surface and correlating it with their synergistic co-activation using ligands functionalized on lipid bilayers. We confirmed that co-activation of TLR4 and Fc{gamma}R enhances whole-cell pro-inflammatory responses and tyrosine phosphorylation at the receptor level. Super-resolution microscopy revealed that TLR4 and Fc{gamma}R each form discrete nanoclusters after ligand stimulation, and their synergistic co-activation significantly increases both the size and spatial overlap of these nanoclusters, leading to amplified immune signaling. Contrary to previous assumptions that TLR4 and Fc{gamma}R form heterodimers during their crosstalk, our results emphasize the critical role of receptor nanocluster interactions in modulating innate immune responses. Additionally, these findings align with similar receptor interaction mechanisms that we previously reported in other receptor pairs, such as Dectin-1/TLR2 and Fc{gamma}R/TLR2, suggesting that nanocluster interactions may represent a predominant mechanism governing crosstalk between TLRs and ITAM-containing receptors.

Bona fide Kupffer cells (KCs) are prenatally seeded and show unique functional and immunophenotypic features among tissue macrophages. They are considered as terminally differentiated, and adaptability in disease is attributed to recruited, monocyte-derived KCs. Here, we investigated the extent of KC plasticity and the impact of origin in mycobacterial infections that target macrophages and can persist for months. Fate-mapping combined with high-resolution imaging revealed the emergence of a unique, infection specific KC subset which downregulated the signature markers CLEC4F and VSIG4 ("KClow"). KClow were derived from bona fide KCs and located exclusively to granuloma cores. In contrast, monocyte-derived macrophages were contained at the granuloma borders and contributed to this tissue reaction. ATAC and single-cell RNA sequencing identified a specific signature of KClow with high antimycobacterial activity and specialization to a hypoxic microenvironment. Despite their fundamental deviation from the classical KC phenotype, KClow showed remarkable adaptability, and were capable to return to a homeostatic-like KC state. Accordingly, mycobacterial infections unmask KCs as highly plastic cells, capable of responding to extreme environmental changes.

Polymorphonuclear lymphocytes (PMNs) are terminally differentiated phagocytes with pivotal roles in infection, inflammation, tissue injury, and resolution. PMNs can display a breadth of responses to diverse endogenous and exogenous stimuli, making understanding of these innate immune responders vital yet challenging to achieve. Here, we report a 22-color spectral flow cytometry panel to profile primary human PMNs on population and single cell levels for surface marker expression of activation, degranulation, phagocytosis, migration, chemotaxis, and interaction with fluorescently labeled cargo. We demonstrate the surface protein response of PMNs to phorbol ester stimulation compared to untreated controls in an adherent PMN model with additional analysis of intra- and inter-subject variability. PMNs challenged with the Gram-negative bacterial pathogen Neisseria gonorrhoeae revealed infectious dose-dependent changes in surface marker expression in bulk, population-level analysis. Imaging flow cytometry complemented spectral cytometry, demonstrating that fluorescence signal from labeled bacteria corresponded with bacterial burden on a per-cell basis. Spectral flow cytometry subsequently identified surface markers which varied with direct PMN-bacterium association as well as those which varied in the presence of bacteria but without phagocytosis. This spectral panel protocol highlights best practices for efficient customization and is compatible with downstream approaches such as spectral cell sorting and single-cell RNA-sequencing for applicability to diverse research questions in the field of PMN biology.

Summary SentenceHere we report a 22-color spectral flow cytometry panel to profile primary human PMNs for markers of activation, degranulation, phagocytosis, migration, and chemotaxis using phorbol ester stimulation and bacterial challenge as proofs-of-concept.

Microscale engagement of the hemi-ITAM-containing receptor Dectin-1 by a fungus-derived particle initiates signaling through the Src-family kinases (SFKs) and Syk that leads to downstream Erk and Akt activation and the macrophage anti-microbial response. To minimize local tissue damage in the absence of a true pathogenic threat, macrophages must remain unresponsive to low-valency receptor ligation by soluble ligands from food or remote infection sites. To investigate how SFKs regulate macrophage sensitivity, we compared signaling in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) exposed to depleted zymosan, a particulate and highly multivalent Dectin-1 ligand, with signaling after pharmacologically induced SFK activation without receptor engagement or formation of a phagocytic synapse. We show that high-valency Dectin-1 engagement and formation of a phagocytic synapse restrict phosphorylation of the ITIM-associated phosphatase SHIP1 and promote Erk and Akt signaling. In contrast, SFK activation in the absence of a phagocytic synapse induces phosphorylation of SHIP1 and leads to dampened activation of Erk and Akt. Whereas multiple SFKs are capable of phos-phorylating SHIP1 in principle, the SFK Lyn functions uniquely in maintaining steady-state phosphorylation of SHIP1 and setting tonic and induced levels of Erk and Akt phosphorylation. Consequently, Lyn has a special role in suppressing the Akt pathway and maintaining Erk/Akt pathway balance. Interestingly, formation of a phagocytic synapse circumvents this requirement for Lyn to maintain Erk/Akt balance. These findings highlight the unique function of Lyn in maintaining mac-rophage steady-state signaling and limiting pro-inflammatory responses to disorganized pathway activation and soluble microbial components.

SUMMARY PARAGRAPHAn effective immune system must sample and appreciate healthy-self identity to prevent autoimmunity and to contrast to pathogenic insults1-3. Self-proteins are presented to T cells in the thymus during immune cell development2,3, and must be presented throughout the body to both maintain regulatory T cell populations4-6 and provide a tonic signal to maintain conventional T cells over time7-9. The ready observations of continuous apoptosis in some organs together with the ingestion of that material by myeloid populations has led to a conventional understanding of ongoing cell-death as a major source of self-antigens10, complemented in some situations by uptake of free-floating cell-derived vesicles. Here, we used a series of companion imaging and vesicular labeling technologies to reveal an alternate process undertaken by macrophages that results in non-destructive and direct sampling of living cells. The process requires cell-cell contact, does not require caspase activation, and takes place via a trogocytosis-like stretching of the target cell into the macrophage, leading to the generation of submicron-sized vesicles containing cytoplasm. Using a high-dimensional flow-based method for labeling vesicles ingested under this versus other conditions, we find that live-sampled material is distinctly processed, is poorly subject to fusion with lysosomes, and produces ensuing differential effects on the presentation of those to CD4 versus CD8 T cells. This demonstrates an important and substantial sampling of living cells by the immune system, with clear consequences for maintaining the border of immunity.

sample_q_texts: Protease-antiprotease complexes play central roles in biological processes such as protein translation and translation elongation. The kinetics and inhibition mechanisms of such interactions have long been the subject of study. In contrast, the hitherto low success rate of protease in vitro screening methods - such as sodium dodecyl sulfate electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) or neuraminidase (NI)-based purification - for interactions with N-termini of polypeptides has hindered structural and mechanistic insights into the two-component relationship that has long been seen to govern protein oligomerization and structure formation. We identified a small RNA (sRNA) that inhibits the native oligomeric state of polyproteins and its cleavage by poly(A)-binding protein 1 (PABPO1). This sRNA functions as an anti-extender protein and co-localizes with the protease, prion-like kinase (PLK), resulting in a translational block. We used a series of computational and biochemical strategies to produce proteins and sRNAs that can block native and processed protein oligomerization and have described their interactions with PLK and N-terminal end-binding protein (NET-B). Our work provides evidence for a crucial role of pan-peptide molecules such as snipe1 in limiting the hybrid state of PLK-polyproteins and producing N-terminal PLK peptides, a biochemical step for which numerous sRNAs have been isolated.

Transfer RNA (tRNA) is the primary molecular tool for decoding messenger RNA (mRNA), facilitating the translation of amino acids into proteins. In this study, we present code-free tRNA prediction based on a pre-trained foundation model. We validated our method by testing a dataset with 504 sequencing specimens. At an RNA count of 1 base per codon, our model achieved an average accuracy of 71.7%.

Micro-RNA (miRNA) motifs display highly conserved biophysical properties that facilitate accurate detection and quantification of miRNA interactions. Particularly, the complementarity between stem-loop pairs or  stem-stem motifs and nucleotides within the loop is vital for the identification of unique miRNA-dependent interactions. While discrete stem-stem motifs have been previously identified and recently proposed, the structure of other conserved C-terminal types remains underexplored, even though a longer miRNA cap that ends with the conserved sequence -39 significantly alters miRNA properties. This research demonstrates that the P1 stem-loop motif is routinely composed of a D-loop flanked by a C-loop, and highlights the critical role of  GU-UG that distinguishes the structures of mature and un-mature small interfering RNAs (sRNAs) and miR-1. In so doing, it advances the understanding of stem-loop structures for long-read capture of sRNAs and 3UTR-mediated miRNA silencing in Escherichia coli cells.

RNA can contain stop codon blockages during replication. The non-synonymous (NS) variants at the recognized genetic stop codon sites are proposed to protect against codon biases or degrade the overall rate of the genome; the synonymous (NS) variants enable the fine-tuning of codon usage in this context. Whether certain deviations in the evolution of secondary and stop codon patterns could arise from the NS-related selectivity and whether they have consequences for the reading rate under an error-prone scenario will be addressed in this work. An in-depth analysis of the influence of genetic stop codes on the whole-genome mapping of the difference between the conserved versus the newly evolved DNA sequences is presented. The consequences of evolutionary changes in the codon bias for genome mapping will be discussed based on the examples of Ortho-au-bach sequences that differ significantly in their stop codon blocks. Possible adverse consequences of nucleotide constraints, the evolutionary rate of nucleotide substitutions, and NS selection and associated outcome will also be assessed. The latter is addressed with short RNA replicons, in which only NS-selective replacements for tandem repeats are inserted in RNA. The resulting replicons display significantly lower base reading rates in comparison to reference cellular RNA replicons. This analysis may be a helpful benchmark for future studies of stop codons and their ecological role and target specificity in natural RNA sequences.

A key missing part of the mRNA sequence arsenal is the capability to specify the precise articulation between the sequence encoding a  rRNA and the protein of interest. The human natural repertoire is a primary source for rRNAs and consists of two large non-regulatory single-stranded RNA elements for each of the two non-coding RNA (ncRNA) classes. Here, we profile sequence evolution, genomically-characterized and functionally annotated members of the human natural repertoire. We use ncRNA features, mapped using metagenome sequencing, to build on the previously published assessment of diverse features, such as two-nucleotide patterns, canonical N4P motifs, and two-middle-successive-norestringence patterns, to identify those that effectively track a protein of interest. Here we show that sequence, general transcription factor and feedback loops are common attributes that profile genes in the ncRNA repertoire. We additionally find that consensus adenosines and guanines in the 4-end of these  RNA units correlates with higher availability of previously reported or more likely contributing to the function in human cells of human ribonucleases. Collectively, these efforts allow us to harness sequence information from the human natural repertoire as a general, adaptable tool for rationally tuning proteome-level expression.

RNA molecules undergo numerous types of secondary structures. Identifying and understanding the role of RNA secondary structures is a major goal for biological research. In conventional methods, RNA molecules are modeled by static atomic coordinates, and therefore secondary structures are only considered when the backbone is fixed. Here, we investigate variations to this structure. Specifically, we focus on a method called RCMDAL to model RNA secondary structures. We conduct an empirical analysis of this method using various datasets and present results. This work shows that RNA structures can significantly change with fixed backbone coordinates while retaining much of their structure, as well as that neglecting RNA secondary structures creates discrepancies between experiments and simulations.

Introns, non-coding genomic sequences that are transcribed and localized to mRNA intermediates, pose significant challenges to theoretical models of genetic information storage. One critical question concerns the mechanism of intron detection, given that a non-coding sequence is always selected to accommodate a non-functional information content. Here we develop an analytical framework to explore the temporal evolution of the proportion of non-intron sequences in a genomic code under various mechanisms for intron detection. We find that for a very permissive detector, considered here to be analogous to no introns, the sequence will soon be deleted, driven by cost minimization and mutations. Intron detection alters the coding laws in many unexpected ways, including reducing the fraction of codons and genes with a zero GC content and exposing codons to deleterious mutations. Although each of these effects can be alleviated by modifying the underlying mechanism for intron detection, the resulting system for coding information remains exceedingly stable. This theoretical study reveals the link between the relationship between function and structure in genomic information processing, providing a foundational understanding of the limits of genetic information storage in any biological system.

Large-scale molecular biology involves the sequencing of an ensemble of nucleic acids, protein, or other complex molecules to obtain the raw sequence data. For the abundance of genomic data accumulating each year, producing many short nucleotide sequences leads to data loss and noise, and, consequently, lower data quality. Particularly problematic is the use of nucleotide substitutions when performing short read alignment, which is widely used for downstream processing tasks. Accurate substitution models, referred to as prediction models, can improve the accuracy of alignment while improving data quality. However, these prediction models have never been evaluated for their performance under a different set of conditions, and thus, these models remain largely untested. In this work, we proposed two non-negative matrix factorization models for nucleotide substitutions. The models require, as input, short reads with and without indels, resulting in unique alignments between the sequences after the substitution and their respective original sequences. We demonstrated that the projection of data into a few principal components can minimize noise and enhance sequence integrity, improving the alignment accuracy compared to the Euclidean projection. However, the alignment accuracy is more sensitive to the noise variance, where small misalignment can lead to a large error in the predicted substitution. Our findings revealed the versatility of the proposed models, which offers a clear explanation for measurement of alignment noise in substitution modeling.

Polypeptides span from 100 to 4000 residues long, but only a limited number of proteins is typically built on the core of that range, e.g. insulin is built on the core 800-1200 residues long, and myoglobin is built on the core of 2000. Unraveling the amino-acid composition of protein precursor is a crucial first step to understand protein architecture, structure, and function, which often relies on protein science to unravel. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins and ribosomes translate those amino acids to peptides and eventually to long proteins by eliminating non-amino acids or nonsense codons. While looking at the rule of efficient decoding, the variations within the code that allow an extra passage of amino-acids have been explored for a long time. However, recent advances in measuring mutations in proteins directly on the backbone of the RNA complex, the ribosome, has uncovered that amino acids have a greater effect in protein fold and function than the cells decoding rules. To advance studying protein into a decoding language view, we introduce an experimental approach based on reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography, which is capable of detecting the amino-acids present in the genome that impact the assembly of protein by removing them. By utilizing this method, we find that all of the core amino acids, C2-C5 and C6-C8 on the ribosome, have significant impacts on peptide folding and structural dynamics. However, the most impact comes for the C1,13-C2,18 residues, which we identified to be the most abundant residues in the proline-rich proteins, with similar findings across proteins. Many biological functions rely on those proteins and which we will propose to be the most abundant residues of the 2800-4000 are used during protein evolution and folding. More specifically, our statistical analyses from changing amino-acid in multiple domains of the ribosome, the peptide synthesis zone and the decoding zone of the ribosome, reveals a distribution of amino acids that optimizes for enhancing correctness of decoding specific reading frames from a given genomic sequence. Additionally, our theoretical models capture all experimental data, and with a few parameters also suggest how post-translation modifications of proteins and protein folding are informed by the amino-acid sequence.

Transmembrane protein evolution through convergent sequence divergence is a common strategy in eukaryotic genomes. Degraded translation, RNA editing and/or splicing can occur during evolution, leading to a longlist of transmembranes that are almost exclusively made of the same protein, and may even co-exist in a physiological state. The messenger RNA editing enzymes acting in cilia can be restricted to the transmembrane domain and are thus usually targeted by ribosomes, preventing the continuous presence of ribosomal damage. Here, we tested the transmembranous nature of transitional RNAs produced in a completely random genome. The results showed that the presence of "ribosomes" did not affect the editing rate, remaining only slightly lower than for other exogenous RNAs without ribosomes. We propose that ribosomes exert an adaptive selection pressure on this form of transcript. In parallel, the transmembranous nature of miRNA editing seems to be maintained over transmembranous ones through endonucleolytic and ribonuclease editing. These findings expand the current understanding of the presence of ribosomes in eukaryotic cells, along with transmembranous RNA editing.
sample_p_texts: A ribozyme that can charge a tRNA with amino acids and discriminate between cognate and non-cognate tRNAs is of interest because a RNA with this ability may have been a critical for translation in the transition from the RNA world. In addition, it could provide a tool for incorporating non-canonical amino acids for biotechnology applications. Here, we rationally engineer a ribozyme by fusing a tRNA binding module (a T-box riboswitch) with a catalytic module (a flexizyme) to generate a ribozyme that can amino acylate a target tRNA. We demonstrate that this ribozyme be readily redesigned to alter tRNA specificity. This ribozyme is compatible with an in vitro translation system and could be used to recode a protein sequence to site-specifically incomporate a non-canonical amino acid.

The functions of non-coding RNAs are largely defined by their three-dimensional structures. RNA 3D structure is organized hierarchically and consists of recurrent building blocks called tertiary motifs. The computational problem of RNA tertiary motif search remains largely unsolved, as standard approaches are restrained by sequence, interaction network, or backbone topology. We developed the ARTEM superposition algorithm, which is free from these limitations. Here, we present a version of ARTEM that allows automated searches of RNA and DNA structure databases to identify 3D structure motifs. We exemplify it by a search of motifs isosteric to the kink-turn motif. This widespread motif plays a role in many aspects of RNA function, and its mutations are known to cause several human syndromes. With ARTEM, we discovered two new kink-turn topologies, multiple no-kink variants of the motif, and showed that a ribosomal junction in bacteria forms either a kink or a no-kink variant depending on the species. Additionally, we identified kink-turns in the catalytic core of group II introns, whose structures have not previously been characterized as containing kink-turns. ARTEM opens a fundamentally new way to study RNA and DNA 3D folds and motifs and analyze their correlations and variations.

Sequence design is the critical first step in developing a new mRNA medicine. The mRNA primary sequence is assembled from multiple elements, including the coding sequence of the target protein or gene, flanking untranslated regions that impact expression, and the poly(A) tail, which improves stability. The mRNA primary sequence can be optimized to improve the performance of an mRNA medicine, including increasing translation and stability, and reducing reactogenicity. Here, we introduce mRNArchitect, a software toolkit to assist in the design of mRNA sequences. mRNArchitect can rapidly assemble and optimize mRNA sequences based on user requirements, including GC content, secondary structure, codon optimization, and uridine depletion. The sequences generated by mRNArchitect can also be readily synthesized, and have been experimentally validated across a variety of applications. We present mRNArchitect as a software toolkit to help scientists design new mRNA medicines.

Availability and implementationmRNArchitect is available via a web portal at www.basefacility.org.au/software/ and Github at https://github.com/BaseUQ/mRNArchitect. mRNArchitect is open-source and freely available under MIT License.

The complexity in the generation of RNA multiple sequence alignments and assessment of the accuracy of such alignments contributes to the challenges in the utilization of RNA alignments in diverse integrative methods. RNAhub is a freely available user-friendly web server for a reliable generation of RNA multiple sequence alignments and the detection of the presence of structural RNA utilizing evolutionary information. This web-based tool, developed by the integration of existing computational approaches, takes an RNA sequence as input and automatically retrieves and aligns sequences homologous to the input (query) RNA sequence through an iterative and structure-agnostic approach. Based on the alignment, this tool statistically assesses whether the query RNA sequence has a conserved RNA structure using covariation analysis. The web server allows the user to efficiently search the sequence of interest against carefully curated, ready-to-use genomic databases to produce a multiple sequence alignment. Using this alignment, our tool either detects the presence of a conserved structural RNA, finds evidence against the presence of a conserved structure, or cannot make any assessment due to a lack of sequence diversity in the alignment. The web server is freely available at https://rnahub.org.

Splicing of introns is an important step that pre-mRNA transcripts undergo during processing in the nucleus to become mature mRNAs. Although long thought to occur in a single step, introns are now also known to be removed in multiple steps through a process called recursive splicing. This non-canonical form of splicing is hypothesized to increase splicing fidelity, particularly in longer introns. In species that have evolved gigantic genome sizes, overall intron lengths are much longer than in genomes of typical size. Using West African lungfish (Protopterus annectens; genome size [~]40Gb) as a model, we use total RNA-seq data to test the hypothesis that gigantic genomes have shifted to rely predominantly on recursive splicing to manage their long introns. Our results suggest levels of recursive splicing at conserved sites in the lungfish that are similar to those seen in humans, indicating that genome-wide intronic expansion accompanying genomic gigantism does not necessitate ubiquitous use of recursive splicing. However, in addition to these results, we also observed patterns of decreasing RNA-seq read depths across entire intron lengths and note that both canonical co-transcriptional splicing and stochastic recursive splicing using many random splice sites could produce this pattern. Thus, we infer canonical co-transcriptional splicing and/or stochastic recursive splicing - but not ubiquitous recursive splicing at conserved sites - manage the removal of long introns in gigantic genomes. We conclude that the vast increase in intron length in gigantic genomes does not appear to have coincided with a fundamental shift in splicing mechanisms.

Cellular RNA levels are a product of synthesis and degradation kinetics, which can differ among transcripts of the same gene. An important cause of isoform-specific decay is the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, which degrades transcripts with premature termination codons (PTCs) and other features. Understanding NMD functions requires strategies to quantify isoform kinetics; however, current approaches remain limited. Methods like nucleotide-recoding RNA-seq (NR-seq) enable insights into RNA kinetics, but existing bioinformatic tools do not provide robust, isoform-specific degradation rate constant estimates. We extend the EZbakR-suite by implementing a strategy to infer isoform-level kinetics from short-read NR-seq data. This approach uncovers unexpected variability in NMD efficiency among transcripts with conserved PTC-containing exons and rapid decay of a subset of mRNAs lacking PTCs. Our findings highlight the effects of competition between NMD and other decay pathways, provide mechanistic insights into established NMD efficiency correlates, and identify transcript features promoting efficient decay.

Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are short dynamic regions of proteins, stabilizing through interactions with other protein residues. IDRs play a role in cell cycle progression and response to cell environment such as nutrients. However, the precise mechanisms by which these interactions occur remain unknown. Here, we analyze disordered regions by segmenting them based on amino acid types. We find that protein-protein interactions for disordered regions follow a hierarchical mapping, where we consider all protein residues as subsets and each segment based on their pairwise interactions to capture greater detail than full IDRs. From this we identify that protein-protein interactions increase with protein IDR concentration. Furthermore, that molecular recognition occurs via a mechanism that does not require co-purification prior to fragmentation, indicating that disordered regions do not require prior macromolecular assembly to occur. In summary, we demonstrate that disordered protein regions couple with associated protein interactions, providing insights into the stability of disordered regions.

Author summaryProtein IDRs occur at the domains of disordered proteins that promote protein-protein interactions and coupling to those interactions, but they are often not studied. We find that IDRs grow in concentration with protein and protein-protein interactions arise, in part, from recognition of what those interactions are between proteins. Here, we found IDR networks increase with protein IDR concentration and the probability of protein-protein interactions is higher in IDRs. Furthermore, prior co-purification can increase the probability of protein-protein interactions in IDRs. In summary, disordered proteins are a ubiquitous component of proteins. We show that IDRs are assembled from disordered regions of proteins and they link to protein interactions in the same way that charge is generally used to represent binding affinities.

Protein secondary structures are critical structural elements in protein function, and enzymes are largely determined by the native folding of the corresponding proproteins. However, 10-30% of human diseases still remain incurable because we have thus far lacked a systematic approach to understand and control protein secondary structure. During recent decades, protein design--a rapidly growing field and one of the fastest-evolving domains of biology--has been revolutionized by machine learning. This section of artificial intelligence (AI) integrates unsupervised modeling, strong interactions (e.g., coding genes or protein monomers or large-scale structures), and efficient search algorithms. Using AI to design proteins has become a new field that is constantly developing rapidly. For example, the protein in Charge 1 which is a vital protein component in human cell metabolism. Charge 1 is predicted to play a key role in immunity in the cytosol of resting cells, but the site where the histidine amino acid chain is attached has not been elucidated. Charge 1 is characterized by the presence of a N-terminal glycine sequence at its active site that is occasionally needed to bind a cofactor, making it a promising protein component for activation of several immunity-linked immune factors.

In the past five years, AI has rapidly progressed in prediction and design of secondary structures. In order to capture the entire complexity of Charge 1 structure, we developed a machine-learning algorithm, XAI2, combining protein designer fusion algorithm, Curie, with fuzzy neural network to predict Charge 1s secondary structures. We tested XAI2 on five Charge 1 motifs, encoded by separate amino acid residues in Charge 1, with three alphas (Gly56, Glu57, Ala157). Our results show that XAI2 successfully predicted the intended alpha-encoded charge 1 motifs by combining sequences from different local Folds. Unlike existing approaches that relied on key features such as motif enrichment, we leveraged the entire sequence space for the Charge 1 protein sequence, extending predictions past common coding information and heavy folding features to the complex structural space of Charge 1. To validate the accuracy of XAI2 and directly compare it with our previous approach, we conducted a manual ranking of previously published mutants. The recognition rate for codons, folds, as well as the number of predicted and curated mutants were high. We found XAI2 to be a promising tool for machine learning-assisted design of the Charge 1 domain.

PARDJ2 is an evolutionarily conserved protease of Huse disease-causing proteins that undergoes phase separation to form amyloid-like structures during development and in neurodegenerative and other diseases. The Rrp9, a GTPase which is important for DNA replication, restricts PARDJ2 during phase separation through ligand binding, changing the conformation of the PARDJ2-Rrp9 interface. This study aims to evaluate how Rrp9 restricts PARDJ2 amyloid formation using complementary proteomics and transcriptomics. Based on proteomics analysis, the Rrp9-PARDJ2 interaction was observed to be specific and involves the inhibition of GTPase activity. To explore the role of GTPase activity in binding PARDJ2 and formation of amyloid structures, we engineered a PARDJ2 mutant (H60S) to express wild-type Rrp9. In this model system, the restricted affinity of wild-type Rrp9, in contrast to Rrp9 in the pHD strain, in combination with the observed effects of Rrp9-PARDJ2 interaction, revealed the conserved nature of the GTPase-mediated conformational change. Moreover, we demonstrated the significance of Rrp9 GTPase activity in interaction with the PARDJ2 F-P motif for hindering GTPases activity. We also identified a conserved proto-helix region on PARDJ2, which was potentially binding site for Rrp9. These findings have implications for GRASM, our newest protein structure prediction algorithm, which utilizes PDB-based string generation, protein interaction modeling and correlation to infer potential site of interaction. Using PDB-based generation of string, we identified a proto-helix region on PARDJ2, which is conserved across species and not necessarily binding to Rrp9. Correlation in deep learning models could help to exclude redundancy, which would improve the accuracy of protein prediction.
