Proteins are key biological units that drive biological functions and are the substrate for virtually every enzymatic reaction in cellular processes. To engineer the expression of proteins, they must first be rationally designed. Computational tools, such as machine learning (ML), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and physics-based approaches, have been used to design proteins without the need to elucidate sequence information. As a result, there are vast amounts of genomic and antibody-derived information for protein design currently available. However, the human body has approximately three million genes compared to the hundreds of genes required for protein design, resulting in the overwhelming amount of information currently available being used for only a very small number of proteins. A genetic code inference system, together with a self-supervised learning system, can approximate the genetic code to a significantly lower precision and lead to useful results in protein design. In this work, we develop an approach leveraging genetic code conversion by genetic code inference to generate a collection of the sequence space of proteins. In doing so, we create a collection that is curated for protein design through self-supervised learning. We find that, in doing so, the experimental results are broadly in agreement with previously designed proteins.

SH3 Domains broadly serve as ligands for SNO Transporters, whose function lies in assisting folding of folding proteins. Motivated by this functional relationship, we employ AlphaFold 3 (AF3) to predict various types of SH3 domains and perform multiple bifurcations to arrive at an exact sequence of folded, stable proteins. Here, we provide practical recommendations for AF3 model generation for uncovering the domains regulatory SH3 domains function, including predictions and sub-structural alignment between several SH3 domains with dual functionalities.

Analysis of dynamics encoded in proteins would greatly facilitate the understanding of protein biogenesis and their contributions in disease development. Integrating biophysics with experimental measurements helps unveil the kinetics encoded in a protein. Recent analyses of a variety of disease-associated proteins or proteins engineered to model them, rely on whole-cell, 3D physical modelling. While these methods lend themselves to analyze protein dynamics, most analyses do not directly interrogate the protein-folding process per se and do not allow assessing the kinetics of the unfolding phase. Here, we present a whole-proteome approach that jointly analyses both the intrinsic folding dynamics and their consequences with the help of a fine-grained, digital-twin model. The digital-twin approach enriches dynamical information encoded in the protein with a fidelity that makes biological analogy understandable. As a first step, we incorporated the previously reported dynamics of the formyl peptide propepsin by using the Digital-Twin Model we devised. We obtained a first principle view of propepsins intrinsic dynamics, which was subsequently complemented with a full 3D structural validation of its digital-twin. Finally, we employed the intrinsic dynamics for phenotyping the Digital-Twin Model protein (anti-propepsin antibody) in the presence of known antibodies. Analyzing the dynamics enriches biophysical characterizations of disease-associated proteins and significantly aids in identifying disease-relevant protein dynamics for the development of biomarkers and therapeutic opportunities.

Intrinsically disordered proteins and proteins (IDPs/IDPs) are small protein domains that play roles in numerous biological processes due to their weak-interactibility with globular proteins. Such IDPs are widely considered to have no underlying structure and need to be modeled as self-assembling systems. Nevertheless, despite their distinct physical properties, there are many IDPs whose structure and potential to form self-assemblies have not been studied. Therefore, our study presents a comprehensive methodology for identification, model preparation, and validation of intrinsically disordered proteins and IDPs. This methodology includes four essential steps: 1) identification of protein sequences by sequence similarity analysis and comparison with databases; 2) definition of protein series model (protein in-frame or frame as a whole); 3) identification of IDPs sequence using a sequence similarity/alignment approach to the same protein sequences as we described in the basic model; and 4) prediction and/or model test (validation) with the set of IDPs sequences. Our findings show that the ability of the proposed analysis approach to identify IDPs from both self-assembling proteins sequences and protein sequence databases has been the first in the field. Furthermore, structural models of protein IDPs can be predicted and validated using the set of IDPs sequence and protein sequence database. This finding suggests that IDPs which are observed in living systems can be used as a marker of protein sequence as well as structures, and thus, is of crucial interest to functional genomics, proteomics, machine learning, nanotechnology, and polymer chemistry.

We developed a novel approach to determine the rate-limiting parameter in splicing repair processes for use in defining a therapeutic signature. High-performance computing has a significant impact on the efficiency of protein-protein interactions and their dynamics. As a result of this discovery, we have created an algorithm for evaluating network-informed mixing, which is an algorithm for integrating the empirical binding network with the adaptive sequence network of proteins. The obtained mixes provide a means of providing deep insights into the interaction dynamics of proteins. In a computationally interesting case, we compared the change in affinity of two proteins under the condition of efficient mixing with their binding strength to each other measured by isopeptide bond connections. The change in affinity indicates that the protein exchange events can promote the affinity. This study is an important step toward the discovery of sequence-based and network-informed profiling of protein interactions with therapeutic biomarkers.

In this study, we discovered the importance of amino acid and peptide sidechain ionization. Alpha-helix and beta-hairpin structures are potential targets for designing peptides by exploiting ionization efficiency. The study examines the potential impact of alanine, glycine, cysteine, hydroxyethyllysine, and serine sidechain ionizations using Computational Hard Folding (CHF) and Deep Learning Models (DLMs). Using a data set that includes 3560 entries, the models are utilized to predict the ionization efficiency of these sidechain ionizations for proteins of varying lengths. Through a comparative analysis, the findings indicate that advanced computational methods using high-throughput computing techniques can be used to predict the ionization efficiency of sidechains. Currently, only a few of them have been studied in the body of knowledge, which makes further research necessary. Further research is also needed to understand how functional residues can be predicted and the potential to use these methods for de novo protein design.

AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWRecent years have witnessed a significant evolution of automated metabolic annotation approaches. Among them, the widely-used Brookhaven Challenge (BC) competition, which challenges automated methods to annotate whole and partly annotated genomes of protein molecules, has had a strong impact on the field. Here, we track these developments by analysing the challenges submitted since its inception. We estimate the number of proteins annotated by each methodological improvement, the number of protein families annotated by at least one improvement, the cost of submission (via funding provided by co-authors) and various ancillary tasks (alignment, false detection, experimental validation, missing annotations) performed over the last 14 years. We further evaluate the accuracy of newly adopted statistical approaches and chart the presence of false discoveries in experimentally verified alternative mechanisms of action. Based on this, we argue for a realistic view of the current state-of-the-art of automated metabolic annotation and to what extent contributions of BC and surrounding community result in fact improved annotation accuracy.
sample_p_texts: Protein pKa prediction is a key challenge in computational biology. In this study, we present pKALM, a novel deep learning-based method for high-throughput protein pKa prediction. pKALM uses a protein language model (PLM) to capture the complex sequence-structure relationship of proteins. While traditionally considered a structure-based problem, our results show that a PLM pre-trained on large-scale protein sequence databases can effectively learn this relationship and achieve state-of-the-art performance. pKALM accurately predicts the pKa values of six residues (Asp, Glu, His, Lys, Cys, and Tyr) and two termini with high precision and efficiency. It excels at predicting both exposed and buried residues, which often deviate from standard pKa values measured in solvent. We demonstrate a novel finding that predicted protein isoelectric points (pI) can be used to improve the accuracy of pKa prediction. High-throughput pKa prediction of the human proteome using pKALM achieves a speed of 4,965 pKa predictions per second, which is several orders of magnitude faster than existing state-of-the-art methods. The case studies illustrate the efficacy of pKALM in estimating pKa values and the constraints of the method. pKALM will thus be a valuable tool for researchers in the fields of biochemistry, biophysics, and drug design.

As classic evaluation indexes, clustering-wise predictive positive value (PPV) and accuracy (ACC) have been widely used for the detection of protein complexes ([1]). However, we identified a critical error in their calculation, which can lead to inaccurate evaluation results under most conditions. Here, we elaborate on the problem of the original indexes and propose revised indexes PPVM (PPV Modified) and ACCM, which correct the identified error. Experiments demonstrate that revised indexes achieve higher reliability. Based on the new indexes, we reevaluated three state-of-the-art computational methods for protein complex detection on five benchmarks to provide a revised baseline to facilitate comparison of performance for algorithms developed later. The code and data involved in the experimental section of this paper can be found in https://github.com/hyx-1/PPV_M-and-ACC_M.

Recombinant protein expression can be a limiting step in the production of protein reagents for drug discovery and other biotechnology applications. We introduce RP3Net (Recombinant Protein Production Prediction Network), an AI model of small-scale heterologous soluble protein expression in Escherichia coli. RP3Net utilizes the most recent protein and genomic foundational models. A curated dataset of internal experimental results from AstraZeneca (AZ) and publicly available data from the Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) was used for training, validation and testing of RP3Net. Set Transformer Pooling (STP) aggregation and Meta Label Correction (MLC) with large scale purification data enabled RP3Net to improve Area Under Receiver Operator Curve (AUROC) by 0.15, compared to the baseline model. When experimentally validated on an independent, manually selected set of 97 constructs, RP3Net outperformed currently available models, with an AUROC of 0.83, delivering accurate predictions in 77% of the cases, and correctly identifying successfully expressing constructs in 92% of cases.

Advances in computational and experimental methods have revealed the existence of transient, non-native protein folding intermediates that could play roles in disparate biological processes, from regulation of protein expression to disease-relevant misfolding mechanisms. Here, we tested the possibility that specific post-translational modifications may involve residues exposed during the folding process by assessing the solvent accessibility of 87,138 post-translationally modified amino acids in the human proteome. Unexpectedly, we found that one-third of phosphorylated proteins present at least one phosphosite completely buried within the proteins inner core. Computational and experimental analyses suggest that these cryptic phosphosites may become exposed during the folding process, where their modification could destabilize native structures and trigger protein degradation. Phylogenetic investigation also reveals that cryptic phosphosites are more conserved than surface-exposed phosphorylated residues. Finally, cross-referencing with cancer mutation databases suggests that phosphomimetic mutations in cryptic phosphosites can increase tumor fitness by inactivating specific onco-suppressors. These findings define a novel role for co-translational phosphorylation in shaping protein folding and expression, laying the groundwork for exploring the implications of cryptic phosphosites in health and disease.

Stability is a key factor to enable the use of recombinant proteins in therapeutic or biotechnological applications. Deep learning protein design approaches like ProteinMPNN have shown strong performance both in creating novel proteins or stabilizing existing ones. However, it is unlikely that the stability of the designs will significantly exceed that of the natural proteins in the training set, which are biophysically only marginally stable. Therefore, we collected predicted protein structures from hyperthermophiles, which differ substantially in their amino acid composition from mesophiles. Notably, ProteinMPNN fails to recover their unique amino acid composition. Here we show that a retrained network on predicted proteins from hyperthermophiles, termed HyperMPNN, not only recovers this unique amino acid composition but can also be applied to proteins from non-hyperthermophiles. Using this novel approach on a protein nanoparticle with a melting temperature of 65{degrees}C resulted in designs remaining stable at 95{degrees}C. In conclusion, we created a new way to design highly thermostable proteins through self-supervised learning on data from hyperthermophiles.

We present a unified framework for protein reactive-site prediction that couples a rigorous geometric, quantum-inspired model with a metal-aware, fully deterministic implementation. Proteins are treated as smooth Riemannian manifolds; each residue is equipped with a localized fiber, whose environment vector encodes geometric and physico-chemical features. Motivated by Density Functional Theory--which links global electron density to reactivity--we hypothesize that a sufficiently rich local density stencil captures the same information at the residue scale. On this foundation we build a single-file Python toolkit, reactive_site_predictor.py, which ranks candidate reactive residues in both metallo- and apo-proteins. The score combines (i) a geometry-based environment term, (ii) relativistic ZORA distance factors for metal centers, (iii) coordination-number and angle-deviation corrections, and (iv) an optional pocket-proximity flag. A fixed global random seed removes all stochastic elements, guaranteeing reproducibility. Benchmarks on three representative assemblies--Rubisco, GroEL, and SecA--achieve top-10 recall between 90 and 50 percent for documented functional residues. While promising, the current validation is limited to three static PDB structures; extension to dynamic ensembles and explicit quantum layers is left to future work. The framework thus offers an interpretable, physics-grounded, and deterministic paradigm for protein-function prediction. Beyond residue-level reactivity, the same manifold-fiber formalism is ultimately intended for purely geometric analysis of protein-protein interfaces : instead of assigning scalar scores, we construct an explicit contact sub-manifold and study its curvature, topology, and fibre-overlap signatures to deduce interaction logic without additional learning. Benchmarks on sixteen diverse protein assemblies (three originals + thirteen new targets) show top-10 recall between 50%and 100 %, underscoring the frameworks generality. Across the full benchmark of sixteen proteins, the method recovers 134 literature-supported residues among 160 top-rank predictions, corresponding to a global Top-10 precision of 0.84.

Protein S-palmitoylation is a reversible lipophilic posttranslational modification regulating a diverse number of signaling pathways. Within transmembrane proteins (TMPs), S-palmitoylation is implicated in conditions from inflammatory disorders to respiratory viral infections. Many small-scale experiments have observed S-palmitoylation at juxtamembrane Cys residues. However, most large-scale S-palmitoyl discovery efforts rely on trypsin-based proteomics within which hydrophobic juxtamembrane regions are likely underrepresented. Machine learning- by virtue of its freedom from experimental constraints - is particularly well suited to address this discovery gap surrounding TMP S-palmitoylation. Utilizing a UniProt-derived feature set, a gradient boosted machine learning tool (TopoPalmTree) was constructed and applied to a holdout dataset of viral S-palmitoylated proteins. Upon application to the mouse TMP proteome, 1591 putative S-palmitoyl sites (i.e. not listed in SwissPalm or UniProt) were identified. Two lung-expressed S-palmitoyl candidates (synaptobrevin Vamp5 and water channel Aquaporin-5) were experimentally assessed. Finally, TopoPalmTree was used for rational design of an S-palmitoyl site on KDEL-Receptor 2. This readily interpretable model aligns the innumerable small-scale experiments observing juxtamembrane S-palmitoylation into a proteomic tool for TMP S-palmitoyl discovery and design, thus facilitating future investigations of this important modification.

PRoteolysis TArgeting Chimeras (PROTACs) can inhibit protein activity by utilizing natural proteasomal degradation pathways for the degradation of target proteins. Being able to determine the degradation potential of PROTACs is crucial in drug development as it can lead to time, labor and cost savings. In this paper, we present a novel machine-learning pipeline that utilizes common compound fingerprints and a pre-trained graph neural network for the prediction of half-maximal degradation concentration of PROTACs by benchmarking a variety of protein tertiary structures and chemical features. Based on critical analysis of our cross-validation and independent test results, we have highlighted several key challenges underlying this prediction problem that need to be addressed to improve the generalization of predictive models in this domain. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by testing it on two different datasets and show that it performs better than the current state of the art with an AUC-ROC of 0.85 and accuracy of 0.875 on the DeepPROTACs test dataset.

sample_q_texts: Low-coverage sequencing (LCS) has spurred significant interest in recent years in assessing basic evolutionary history of a population. In contrast to conventional phylogenetic approaches, where nucleotide diversity and substitution rates must be inferred from comparisons of aligned DNA sequences, LCS offers an alternative approach by measuring the similarity between an alignment and a strand of DNA sequence variations without the need for multiple alignments. Modern LCS approaches can produce posterior estimates of base frequencies, substitution rates, and topology. In this work, we developed LCSNow, a recently developed method for estimating these variables from pseudoreplicates of fragmented genomes of unrelated species, focusing on cpDNA sequences. We propose to estimate these variables and a codon usage preference parameter from pseudoreplicates from bacterial, chlorovirus, and mtDNA reference genomes using the Stochastic Bi-model Methodology that adapts commonly used likelihood-based algorithms for biased bi-model inference. The key innovation of our method is estimating the drift and selection rates using the assumption that the pseudoreplicates are the shortest genetic distance between an organism and its nearest neighbor. We demonstrate the power and flexibility of our approach by applying it to 16 plant species of the Convar database. We found that PseudVibrio parahaemolyticus exhibits a lower probability of evolving codons with the valency of 11 in nucleotides rather than one. We found that PseudVibrio parahaemolyticus has the expected nucleotide bias, whereby in cluster 2p the frequency of G in the 27 non-pseudo nucleotide codon falls the lowest, and in cluster 1a the frequency of T is the highest.

Identifying polymorphisms that discriminate between a gene's ancestral (reference) haplotypes is important for genome-scale predictions, but is often constrained by overlap in haplotypes across related species. Here we propose a novel method using relative haplotypes to infer that ancestral haplotypes are not concordant across unrelated species. The default line of inference that ancestral haplotypes are concordant across related species follows naïve species trees. Instead, we show how resolving relations between pairs of closely related species increases ancestry signatures for ancestral haplotypes by inferring that the best description of derived allele frequencies distinguishes between pairs of related species. For 9,757 crop genetic resources, our best method produces allele frequencies >1 to identify a clade-level ancestry signature in 519 polymorphic markers. For an independently produced complete genome dataset for Arabidopsis thaliana, 99% of ancestral haplotypes are concordant across the species tree, whereas the allele frequency threshold for gene structure inference reduces the genes ancestral signatures to 7%. Class, for example, has an ancestral haplotype signature that identifies 669 classes and the resolution for each class (i.e., the genes that can be inferred to be transcribed, transcribed, or unfocused), thus inferring 266, 2,389, and 633 genes in a genotype from Classis, respectively. Our framework significantly increases the accuracy of gene structure inference and ancestral haplotype identity. Ancestral haplotype inference is available as part of a stand-alone R package: haplotype inference (https://github.com/berkeley-bioinformatics/haplan). To facilitate further development, we include an automatically generated, automatically correct mechanism for detecting error in inferred ancestry signatures.

Short-read assemblies are commonly used for comparative genomics, but quantifying detailed structural variation, or inversions, poses a challenge because most analyses require a highly compressed reference. To overcome this, we present an efficient comparative approach to search large and dense genomic fragments for inversions using key predictions from genome segments. We adapt the strategy to virtual assemblies generated by various assembly generation and analysis tools. Applying our method to one model of Drosophila, we found an inverted gene cluster on the transposable element Trisoma, integrating inversions across 16 chromosomes. We also found inverted genes on other transposable elements such as Elderflower-2 and the non-coding elements Satruna and VRCAM1. Our analysis on three model organisms identified approximately 100 million inversions that vary in size across chromosomes, from 5 to 400 kilobases.

The Method Zone Metrics (MZM) is designed to quantify topological changes in the method zone and estimate the magnitudes of changes in contributing effects by orthological method. The MZM provides a set of metrics (22 total) that are tabulated and available to download on the Methods for Integrative and Comparative Genomics (MAG) website. All MZM metrics are calculated using the minimum gap method; this method compares all methods to their nearest unmapped genomic regions. The corresponding minimum gap metrics are automatically generated through the MZM Program. MZM Metrics spreadsheet (v.2) and accompanying documentation are available from MAG.

The biogenomics revolution has had a profound impact on evolutionary studies, providing a comprehensive view of animal and plant diversity. The field of Biogeography is currently a multidisciplinary discipline, composed of diverse disciplines, such as biogeography, computational biology and ecology, who could benefit from a single computational framework to coordinate and analyze the data generated by each discipline. Currently, the majority of the literature focused on analyzing large-scale maps of whole genome sequencing data, without integrating all sequence types generated by each experiment; nor did they try to simulate the chromosome sizes. Here, we present such a simulation framework, able to integrate phylogenetic, population and genomic data in one computational framework. The computational framework is able to perform a custom analyses, such as structural and gene predictions and similarity measures. We applied the framework to the input data of an previously published paper, allowing to understand the reasons why two genes differ in the same species. We also applied our framework to analyze the Gene Ontology data of 6,560 plants sequenced with Hi-C, to study the genomic difference of the histone deamidase enzymes between plants and fungi. As future work, we plan to expand the Framework to accommodate future input of the custom downstream analysis based on the integrated data.

Pangenome merging is a powerful strategy for constructing large genomes from individual sequences of comparable length. As a result, it can be used to overcome biological and technological challenges posed by complex genomes, such as homopredicates, large repeats, and rare/cluttered genomes, and can generate large genetic variants. However, in practice, producing sizable genomes remains problematic because of the sequence divergence, evolutionary constraints, and data scarcity that separate homopredicates and a lack of data. To address these problems, we apply the newly developed optimization procedure pangenome-merger2, which boosts genome assembly efficiency across multiple genetic datasets. We investigate the performance of pangenome-merger2 by comparing it with three other well-established methods (Pangenome Merder6, UniProt Gather, and Noahsimon) on multiple datasets using simulations, and provide an analysis on the factors affecting their performance. While pangenome-merger2 outperforms other existing methods on most datasets, it is restricted to generating single-chromosome assemblies due to the scarcity of data.

Developing a reliable, fast, accurate, and quantitative method to reconstruct the mitochondrial genome from the histone modifications present at the histone residues that are in direct contact with the DNA double helix is crucial for advancing and standardizing genome annotation workflows. Unlike the standard system for correcting errors in fragmented mitochondrial DNA, which can be achieved with molecular biology tools (e.g., chromosome walking, amplification), no tool exists to date to accurately correct hydrogen bonds while preserving intact DNA sequences and mitochondrial genes. Here, we introduce a new mitochondrial genome reconstruction method, MOGP, which accurately reconstructs the mitochondrial genome from histone modifications data. We describe how MOGP can be performed from histone modification profiles with alignment information or without alignment information. MOGP is a fast, robust, and accurate method that can be used in several scenarios.

Data SummaryMOGP was developed from manually and automatically classified, aligned, and mapped mitochondrial genes and 3,000 intact mitochondrial DNA fragments using mitochondrial genomics data from more than 500 species of fruit, vegetable, and meat. Pvalues were also calculated for at least 16 manually and automatically classified, aligned, and mapped mitochondrial genes. We found that the gap closure rate is high, especially in more rare mitochondrial genes and mitochondrial genes that are not entirely contained in DNA fragments.

The assessment of genomic variability depends on an accurate knowledge of the allele frequency distribution across the genome, which is difficult to quantify without a priori knowledge about the distribution, along with an effective way to quantify and measure such distribution. We propose a method that quantifies and maps allele-frequency distributions using Reach-Quant, a soft-thresholded version of the non-parametric allelic distribution mapping (ADMap) tool. The algorithm assumes that the distribution is sampled from a unimodal distribution with a single null population of steady-state allele frequencies. We also provide a straightforward method to determine unimodal states from reach-spectra obtained from long-range, telomere-to-telomere sequencing. Using our mapping tool for two independent datasets, we find that further from the null allele frequency distribution, the two maps diverge. This divergence increases as the maps get farther away from the null distribution. We show that our mapping of difference-in-mean observed allele frequencies with reach-quant allows a systematic comparison of distances between the models and map their null distribution, and that mapping distance can reveal phylogenetic inference problems.

Quality control in sequence alignment analysis is crucial for robust biological studies. Yet, methods for evaluating alignment quality often rely on visual inspection of alignment graphs, implicitly assuming a uniform distribution of reads across each input sample. However, this approach may overlook sample-specific differences in sequence quality. To address these limitations, we propose to quantify alignment quality by incorporating dynamic binning and alignment statistics, such as uniqueness/length, at each sample site, and further exploiting dynamic binning for sample-to-sample comparison. Our approach allows us to evaluate quality at the sample site level across alignments, without requiring global control metrics, as shown by using chromosome-level analysis in rare cell populations from non-identical human breast tumors. Moreover, our analysis reveals sample-specific correlations between genome assemblies and quality metrics, offering a more realistic understanding of the correlation between reads and alignment quality.

PurposeGenome generalization, using many datasets, has been an effective strategy to generalize from highly correlated genomic distances to datasets with varying distances. Several such approaches have been proposed by incorporating distance estimators such as connected comovement trees and variable resolution statistical mechanics to generate the genome representation, currently generalized into PKMFS. However, a well-studied drawback of these approaches is that the information distribution and connectivity characteristics between the samples are not consistent with the proposed generalization procedures. In this study, we introduce a sample-aware approach to reconstructing sampling information based on genome representation.

MethodsThis study presents a machine learning algorithm that determines from sampled genomic sequences a sample-based representation of the generalized genome. Using two simulation experiments, we show that this sample-aware feature representation is consistent with the proposed generalization procedure.

ResultsWe theoretically indicate that the generated sample-aware representations captured the genetic data's data flow, topological structure, and sampling distribution, which was a common problem of generalization.

ConclusionOur proposed sample-aware feature representation is a promising strategy for capturing the whole genome representation. We hope that this study motivates researchers to consider this innovative strategy for characterizing the importance of information from different regions of genome when generalizing the generalized genome.
sample_p_texts: Long-read single molecule sequencing technologies continue to grow in popularity for genome assembly and provide an effective way to resolve large and complex genomic variants. However, uptake of these technologies for teaching and training is hampered by the complexity of high molecular weight DNA extraction protocols, the time required for library preparation and the costs for sequencing, as well as challenges with downstream data analyses. Here, we present a full long-read workflow optimised for teaching, that covers each stage from DNA extraction, to library preparation and sequencing, to data QC and genome assembly and characterisation, that can be completed in under two weeks. We use a specific case study of plant identification, where students identify an anonymous plant sample by sequencing and assembling the genome and comparing it to other samples and to reference databases. In testing, long-read genome skimming of nine wild-collected plant species extracted with a modified kit-based approach produced an average of 8Gb of Oxford Nanopore data, enabling the complete assembly of plastid genomes, and partial assembly of nuclear genomes. In the classroom, all students were able to complete the protocols, and to correctly identify their plant samples based on BOLD searches of barcoding loci extracted from the plastid genome, coupled with phylogenetic analyses of whole plastid genomes. We supply all the learning material and raw data allowing this to be adapted to a range of teaching settings.

Plant DNA methylation changes occur hundreds to thousands of times faster than DNA mutations and can be transmitted transgenerationally, making them useful for studying population-scale patterns in clonal or selfing species. However, a state-of-the-art approach to use them for inferring population genetic processes and demographic histories is lacking. To address this, we compare evolutionary signatures extracted from CG methylomes and genomes in Arabidopsis thaliana and Brachypodium distachyon. While methylation variants (SMPs) are less effective than single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for identifying population differentiation in A. thaliana, they can classify phenotypically divergent B. distachyon subgroups that are otherwise genetically indistinguishable. The site frequency spectra generated using methylation sites from varied genomic locations and evolutionary conservation exhibit an excess of rare alleles. Nucleotide diversity estimates were three orders of magnitude higher for methylation variants than for SNPs in both species, driven by the higher epimutation rate. Correlations between SNPs and SMPs in nucleotide diversity and allele frequencies at gene exons are weak or absent in A. thaliana, possibly because the two sources of variation reflect evolutionary forces acting at different timescales. Linkage disequilibrium quickly decays within 100 bp for methylation variants in both plant species. Finally, we developed a deep learning-based demographic inference approach. We identified recent population expansions in A. thaliana and B. distachyon using methylation variants that were not identified when using SNPs. Our study demonstrates the unique evolutionary insights methylomes provide that SNPs alone cannot reveal.

Insertions and deletions (indels) are important contributors to the genetic diversity and evolution of pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. However, accurately identifying them from genomic data remains challenging using current variant calling methods. We present skalo, a graph-based algorithm that complements the popular split k-mer approach implemented in the SKA software. skalo is designed for alignment-free inferences of indels between closely related haploid genomes, which are ignored by SKA. The graph traversal implemented in skalo enables rapid detection of indels and complex variants, while retaining the speed and alignment-free advantages of SKA. Through benchmarking on simulated and real Mycobacterium tuberculosis data, we demonstrated its ability to identify indels and complex variants with high precision, and explored their utility as phylogenetic markers to resolve isolates relationships. By providing an efficient and easy-to-use method to extract additional variants from genomic data, skalo can enhance our understanding of pathogen evolution and transmission, with potential applications across diverse pathogen species. skalo is written in Rust and is freely available at https://github.com/rderelle/skalo.

With the explosive growth of whole-genome datasets, the accurate detection of orthologous synteny has become crucial for the reconstruction of evolutionary history. However, the currently available methods for the identification of orthologous synteny have great limitations: the methods are difficult to scale with varying polyploidy histories, and the accurate removal of out-paralogy is challenging. In this study, we developed a scalable and robust approach, the Orthology Index (OI), to identify orthologous synteny. Our evaluation of a large-scale dataset with diverse polyploidization events demonstrated that the technique is highly reliable. This discovery highlights OI as a potentially unified criterion for the identification of orthologous synteny, and this is further validated using simulation-based benchmarks. In addition, we explore its broad applications in reconstructing the evolutionary histories of plant genomes, including inference of polyploidy, identification of reticulation, and phylogenomics. In conclusion, OI offers a robust, interpretable, and scalable approach for identifying orthologous synteny, significantly enhancing our analytical prowess in plant evolutionary genomics.

Our ability to generate sequencing data and assemble it into high quality complete genomes has rapidly advanced in recent years. These data promise to advance our understanding of organismal biology and answer longstanding evolutionary questions. Multiple genome alignment is a key tool in this quest. It is also the area which is lagging: today we can generate genomes faster than we can construct and update multiple alignments containing them. The bottleneck is in considerable computational time required to generate accurate pairwise alignments between divergent genomes, an unavoidable precursor to multiple alignments. This step is typically performed with lastZ, a very sensitive and yet equally slow tool. Here we describe an optimized GPU-enabled pairwise aligner KegAlign. It incorporates a new parallelization strategy, diagonal partitioning, with the latest features of modern GPUs. With KegAlign a typical human/mouse alignment can be computed in under 6 hours on a machine containing a single NVidia A100 GPU and 80 CPU cores without the need for any pre-partitioning of input sequences: a [~]150x improvement over lastZ. While other pairwise aligners can complete this task in a fraction of that time, none achieves the sensitivity of KegAligns main alignment engine, lastZ, and thus may not be suitable for comparing divergent genomes. In addition to providing the source code and a Conda package for KegAlign we also provide a Galaxy workflow that can be readily used by anyone.

Inverted repeats are repetitive elements that can form hairpin and cruciform structures. They are linked to genomic instability, however they also have various biological functions. Their distribution differs markedly across taxonomic groups in the tree of life, and they exhibit high polymorphism due to their inherent genomic instability. Advances in sequencing technologies and declined costs have enabled the generation of an ever-growing number of complete genomes for organisms across taxonomic groups in the tree of life. However, a comprehensive database encompassing inverted repeats across diverse organismal genomes has been lacking. We present InvertiaDB, the first comprehensive database of inverted repeats spanning multiple taxa, featuring repeats identified in the genomes of 118,070 organisms across all major taxonomic groups. The database currently hosts 30,067,666 inverted repeat sequences, serving as a centralized, user-friendly repository to perform searches, interactive visualization, and download existing inverted repeat data for independent analysis. invertiaDB is implemented as a web portal for browsing, analyzing and downloading inverted repeat data. invertiaDB is publicly available at https://invertiadb.netlify.app/homepage.html.

Computational analysis of biological sequences is the cornerstone of modern bioinformatics research. Complex processing and interpretation of data often entails multi-step workflows. The specific requirements and limitations of individual applications can require laborious reformatting and piecemeal  data-wrangling to produce a satisfactory input for each step in a pipeline. We present Squeakuences, a command line tool developed to simplify and automate FASTA file preparation for applications such as phylogenetics, gene annotation, and genome analysis. Implemented in a lightweight Python script, Squeakuences identifies and removes potentially problematic elements in sequence identifiers, such as non-alphanumeric characters, white space, and excessive character count. Squeakuences outputs a new clean version of the sequence file for analysis alongside metadata files to track changes. The user can customize Squeakuences behavior using optional arguments to meet individual processing and formatting requirements. We tested the performance of Squeakuences on molecular data from the human reference genome and found that runtime correlates with the number of sequences processed but not with file size. We expect Squeakuences to save time and manual effort when analyzing sequence data. Squeakuences code is freely available at https://github.com/EvanForsythe/Squeakuences.

Phylogenetic inference is a fundamental problem in biology, which studies the origins and evolutionary relationships among species. Popular phylogenetic inference methods, such as IQ-TREE, RAxML, and PHYML, typically utilize heuristic tree search algorithms to seek a phylogenetic tree that maximizes the likelihood of the observed genetic data. However, tree search is time-consuming and often prone to local optima. To address these issues, we introduce TreeFormer, a new Transformer-based tree rearrangement operation for tree search. Experimental results show that TreeFormer achieves higher accuracy than FastTree 2 when reconstructing trees from real alignments with fewer than 1000 sites.

SummaryTRACK is a user-friendly command-line pipeline designed to consolidate the discovery and comparison of tandem repeats (TRs) across species. TRACK facilitates the cataloging and filtering of TRs based on reference genomes or T2T transcripts, and applies reciprocal LiftOver and sequence alignment methods to identify putative homologous TRs between species. For further streamlined analyses, TRACK can be used to genotype TRs and subsequently estimate and plot basic population genetic statistics. By integrating existing tools into one integrated workflow, TRACK enhances TR analysis accessibility and reproducibility, while offering flexibility for the user.

AvailabilityThe TRACK toolkit with step-by-step tutorial is freely available at https://github.com/caroladam/track.

AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWThe variation of evolutionary histories along the genome presents a challenge for phylogenomic methods to identify the non-recombining regions and reconstruct the phylogenetic tree for each region. To address this problem, many studies used the non-overlapping window approach, often with an arbitrary selection of fixed window sizes that potentially include intra-window recombination events. In this study, we proposed an information theoretic approach to select a window size that best reflects the underlying histories of the alignment. First, we simulated chromosome alignments that reflected the key characteristics of an empirical dataset and found that the AIC is a good predictor of window size accuracy in correctly recovering the tree topologies of the alignment. Due to the issue of missing data in empirical datasets, we then designed a stepwise non-overlapping window approach and applied this method to the genomes of erato-sara Heliconius butterflies and great apes. We found that the best window sizes for the butterflies chromosomes ranged from <125bp to 250bp, which are much shorter than those used in a previous study even though this difference in window size did not significantly change the most common topologies across the genome. On the other hand, the best window sizes for great apes chromosomes ranged from 500bp to 1kb with the proportion of the major topology (grouping human and chimpanzee) falling between 60% and 87%, consistent with previous findings. Additionally, we observed a notable impact of stochastic error and concatenation when using small and large windows, respectively. For instance, the proportion of the major topology for great apes was 50% when using 250bp windows, but reached almost 100% for 64kb windows. In conclusion, our study highlights the challenges associated with selecting a window size in non-overlapping window analyses and proposes the AIC as a more objective way to select the optimal window size for whole genome alignments.

sample_q_texts: Tumors are organized into elongated multiscale cellular territories, referred to as  patches. Emerging evidence indicates that the degree of gene expression overlaps between patches is highly dynamic; however, this patchy structure is frequently neglected in traditional cancer tumor biology. We leveraged highly versatile spatial imaging approaches to resolve the anatomical and molecular organization of 7,252 biopsied patches. This comprehensive approach was applied to the tumor-supporting microenvironment (TME), which was connected to patient-tumor blood-brain barrier (BTB) integrity, to examine the TME architecture of 1,261 patches. We unraveled PATCH (PATHFINDER of COGNITION and Evolved TRIPLET and Its DEPENDENCIES) in which genes across millions of patches are arranged into a scale-dependent architecture. PATTER (PATTER of environment and cell state in tumor) was revealed in which genes across patches are coordinated with each other and cell states via TME composition, implying that these factors evolve in a patch-specific manner. PATCH-responsive regions were identified by integrating patches and TME composition. We reveal that PATCH is expressed within a temperature range corresponding to the TME. We reveal patterns of regions with similar PATCH expression at tumor edges to predict apoptosis during tumor growth. This study provides new insights on how localized genes convey the dynamic landscape of the tumor microenvironment and unveils the potential interaction between TME and PATCH on tumor progression.

Building on the previous work by Rosken, we are developing and deploying mass cytometry for Imaging Immunotherapy (CyMI) (https://github.com/Baird-Siegel-Lab/CyMI). This effort demonstrates the ability of imaging Cytometric Bead Array (CyBA) to show spatial flow cytometry data and enrich sample representativity. We propose open-source software to annotate CyBA images to track tumor growth and drug response and create bone marrow stroma landscape-like images. We anticipate that CyMI will become a widely used tool to study disease-associated cells and stromal cells with machine learning.

Comprehensive spatial transcriptomics (ST) of tumor tissue using Transcriptomics Array Display (TAD) underpins translational cancer research, yet its utility is hampered by complex staining protocols, sample preparation challenges, and variable spatial resolution. We developed MINICAT, a software platform for object-based, image-guided spatial gene expression analysis. Through a series of validations using spatial transcriptomics datasets from breast cancer and prostate cancer, MINICAT provides comprehensive spatial resolution and advanced analysis and visualization of spatial transcriptome data. We show that MINICAT consistently outperforms traditional methods for analyzing multimodal TNM stratification data, simplifying complex spatial transcriptomics data by automating complex analysis workflows.

We provide a user-friendly web-based interface to analyze and visualize the spatial transcriptome data. We showcase a curated dataset of an Invasive Ductal Carcinoma and novel comparative data using normal and malignant breast tumor tissue, including multi-organ spatial patterns of gene expression as well as comparative analysis of TNM stage. By analyzing spatial transcriptome data in contrast to spatial mRNA data, we find many traditional spatial transcriptomics applications to be unfit to analyze other spatial transcriptomics datasets or censoring out of sample spatial transcriptomics data.

De novo states in temporal embryogenesis are mostly structured into  mesoderm and endoderm, with between-tissue differentiation defined by the cell state which them determine cell fate. Information about the genetic basis of these states is scarce due to difficulties in detecting single cells at sufficient resolution to probe intercellular dynamics, but various methodologies have been proposed to overcome this limitation. However, these approaches have either proven less accurate or too computationally demanding. Here we present Dermapix, an approach which combines two existing density-based data analysis methods (Dynamic PopulationSegmentation (DPS) and Compressed Mean Field Projection (CMF) to account for data distortion and heterogeneity, respectively) and present an accurate framework for analyzing single-cell results using DPS with the aim of converting the data into a tractable domain graph. Since this framework does not assume any specific anatomy, it could be potentially applied to other applications.

Single-cell genomics tools, particularly spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing, provide a powerful way of studying individual cells across various tissue contexts. Recent advancements have enabled seamless integration of the two platforms, offering the unique capacity to discern more cell types and quantify diverse parameters associated with gene expression, cell number, and cytoskeletal dynamics. The integration of spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing facilitates studying individual cells residing in varied subcellular locations and measuring gene expression in diverse tissues.

However, integrating these technologies has been fraught with limitations. In particular, high-throughput single-cell spatial transcriptomics images generate massive datasets that are difficult to read due to the complexity and dimensionality of the data. Furthermore, the scale of the resulting datasets poses significant challenges in processing, reading, and analysing. In this study, we present a comprehensive blueprint for processing spatial transcriptomics data. Our workflow aims to assist researchers in developing efficient pipelines for processing single-cell spatial transcriptomics images. Our research combines comprehensive in silico characterisations of cell morphology, gene expression, and stemness, shedding light on the cells interplay with tissue microenvironments and its impact on gene expression and developmental programmes.

Our approach complements existing studies by supporting the analysis of phenotypic data in multiple biological contexts and allows researchers to study how spatial cell and transcriptome environments are modified during embryonic development.

Spatial transcriptomics is an emerging technology that enables real-time cell analysis of tissue structures. The technology has the potential to provide key insights into the in vivo cellular state and function by providing spatial markers of biological structures. RNA-seq was the main technology used for transcriptomic assays, while droplet microfluidics is now a popular method that takes up RNA-seq technology to perform single-cell analyses. These two platforms are often used in parallel to analyse spatially expressed genes in single cells. In contrast, spatial transcriptomics is a single cell platform, but single cell analysis has so far been limited to cells with genetically marked markers (i.e., viral transduction, cell lines). Other cell types not genetically marked often remain unannotated due to the technical constraints of rapid, high-throughput analysis in such high throughput single cell platforms. Here, we describe two methods that enable liquid single cell analysis of cancer cells. First, we define a location-based sampling approach and use it to analyze spatially expressed genes. Second, we extend the methodology by down-sampling single cells via near-infrared fluorescent staining. By combining strategies outlined here, we can provide meaningful spatial and genetic data of cancer cells in situ. Finally, we show that these spatially profiled profiles of cancer cells reliably classify treatment outcomes of patients at a fine spatial level.

Spatial transcriptomics has provided rich information on spatial patterns and dynamics of tissue specific genes. To demonstrate the capabilities of spatial chromatin accessibility data in characterizing transcriptional dynamics of tissues, we systematically developed an open-source spatially-resolved analysis pipeline called the Togus-Haptocela Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis Toolkit (TOST) for human 3D tissues and 2D tissues. The analysis pipeline was applied to humanized bone marrow (BMH) and adipose tissue (Adipo) to unveil spatial chromatin accessibility hierarchies of differentiated hematopoiesis (hematopoietic homeostasis) and adipose tissue in adipose tissue organ-specific damage. Our analysis revealed that chromatin accessibility hierarchies of BMH-specific and Adipo-specific genes are strikingly different from those between the two tissues. First, we profiled 3D regions of BMH and Adipo to distinguish them with respect to differentiation-related genes. We distinguished different differentially regulated regions of bHLH-related genes in BMH-specific versus Adipo-specific programs, which can be implemented as the targets of future precise therapeutic strategies. Second, we corroborated their spatial spatial transcriptomics acquired original data of regulatory sequences, bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs), MSC-to-BMSC differentiation regulatory genes, BMSC-related genes and tissue-specific gene regulatory sequences in each region to draw a more comprehensive picture of differential regulatory mechanisms. We provide TOST to facilitate access to these previously unavailable insights into bMSC-related genes.

AbstractThe high-throughput automation of quantitative Bio-Imaging Inferencing (BI) generates rich data that researchers can use to characterize cell phenotypes. Although manually screened meta-analyses have documented cell heterogeneity, automated methods are indispensable for uncovering patterns such as morphology and gene expression that can reveal biological questions. However, manual screening is time-consuming, particularly for complex phenotypes, and requires substantial expertise in cell biology and signal processing. To address these challenges, we developed "BI-X", a lightweight, easy-to-use machine learning interface that enables non-experts to quickly generate meta-analyses. Here, we demonstrate how "BI-X" is applied to high-dimensional dataset analysis of a complex cell phenotype, as reported herein.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides a spatially resolved view of gene expression in live cells and tissues, typically focusing on single cells. The insights generated from these datasets are enriched by block high-density metabolomics. Yet, ST data often exhibit prohibitive spatial complexity due to technical limitations, challenging the use of in-depth metabolomics to provide meaningful insights. Thus, we introduce the spatial cells extracts (SCE) dataset, a high-resolution spatial transcriptomics-informed ST that incorporates spatially resolved metabolite content across cells. We adopt a spatial query function to interpret SCE snapshots across multiple adjacent tissue samples, enabling cell-type and spatially distinct analyses. Functional validation of SCE datasets in cellular models and tissue samples shows robust activation of targeted genes, validating the spatial characterization of these genes. Similarly, we show that SCE can be used to interrogate spatial tissue-omics in spatial and single cell tissue imaging systems, including Multiview Spectral Tomography. These platforms are available for use with SCE data. The SCE dataset is publicly available and provides an opportunity for comprehensive metabolomic investigations of tissue samples using a spatial query.

We propose sniffy2, an object-based software for extracting single-cell vascular network information from conventional histological images. sniffy2 separates vessels and cells using a contrastive training scheme and performs baseline ancestry correction with a hyper-parameter family that controls the hyper-dimensional distance between different ancestry reconstructions. sniffy2 provides sequence-level copy numbers and experiments with various configurations, mimicking the scaled scale of single-cell genomics methods. We show that sniffy2 enables more precise analysis of spatial effects than current analysis tools and offers additional configuration variables, providing complex experimental designs to scientists, educators, and students.
sample_p_texts: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has shown remarkable promise in pathology applications, shedding light on the spatial organization of gene expression and its relationship to the tumor microenvironment. However, its clinical adoption remains constrained due to the limited scalability of current sequencing technologies. While recent methods attempt to infer ST from whole slide images (WSIs) using pretrained image encoders, they remain restricted by limited gene coverage, organ-specific training, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning. In light of this, we introduce STPath, a generative foundation model pretrained on a large-scale collection of WSIs paired with ST profiles. This extensive pretraining enables STPath to directly predict gene expression across 38,984 genes and 17 organs without requiring downstream fine-tuning. STPath integrates multiple data modalities, including histological images, gene expressions, organ type, and sequencing technology information, within a novel geometry-aware Transformer architecture. Unlike previous methods that directly map WSIs to gene expression, STPath is trained using a masked gene expression prediction objective guided by tailored noise schedules, effectively balancing between capturing gene-gene dependencies and performing high-quality predictions. We evaluate STPath across 6 tasks spanning 23 datasets and 14 biomarkers, including gene expression prediction, spot imputation, spatial clustering, biomarker prediction, gene mutation prediction, and survival prediction. These results demonstrate STPaths strong ability to infer spatially resolved gene expression and reveal crucial pathological structures within tissue samples, underscoring its promise for scalable ST-based pathology applications.

State-of-the-art spatial proteomic and transcriptomic technologies can deeply pheno-type cells in their native tissue environment, providing a high throughput means to effectively quantify spatial relationships between diverse cell populations. However, the experimental design choice of which regions of a tissue will be imaged can greatly impact the interpretation of spatial quantifications. That is, spatial relationships identified in one region of interest may not be interpreted consistently across other regions. To address this challenge, we introduce Kontextual, a method which considers alternative frames of reference for contextualising spatial relationships. These contexts may represent landmarks, spatial domains, or groups of functionally similar cells which are consistent across regions. By modelling spatial relationships between cells relative to these contexts, Kontextual produces robust spatial quantifications that are not confounded by the region selected. We demonstrate in spatial proteomics and spatial transcriptomics datasets that modelling spatial relationships this way is biologically meaningful. We also demonstrate how this approach can be used in a classification setting to improve prediction of patient prognosis.

Advances in spatial profiling have resulted in the generation of multi-omic atlases that span biological scales. In general, multiple workflows are required for image registration, coordinate registration, and spot deconvolution to integrate modalities. To improve the throughput of registration of multi-omic cohorts, we introduce PIVOT, a user-friendly and open-source interface for streamlined nonlinear registration. We demonstrate PIVOTs strengths through registration of three multi-omic datasets, and show comparison of its performance to existing workflows.

The generation of spatial data in biology has been transformed by multiplex imaging and spatial-omics technologies, such as single cell spatial transcriptomics. These approaches permit a detailed mapping of cell populations and phenotypes within the tissue context, which reveals that tissues are complex ecosystems that include multiple organisational structures over different length scales. Quantitative methods for maximising the information that can be retrieved from these images have not kept pace with technological advances in platforms, and no standard methodology has emerged for spatial data analysis. Proposed pipelines are often tailored to individual studies, leading to a fragmented landscape of available methods, and no clear guidance about which statistical tools are best suited to a particular research question.

In response to these challenges, we present MuSpAn, a Multiscale Spatial Analysis package designed to provide straightforward access to well-established and cutting-edge mathematical tools for analysing spatial data. MuSpAn provides easy to use, flexible, and interactive access to quantitative methods developed from mathematical fields that include spatial statistics, topological data analysis, network theory, geometry, probability and ecology. Users can construct custom pipelines from tools across these fields to address specific biological problems, or conduct unbiased exploration of data for discovery spatial biology. In summary, MuSpAn is an extensive platform which enables multiscale analysis of spatial data, ranging from the subcellular to the tissue-scale.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have revolutionized tissue architecture studies by capturing gene expression with spatial context. However, high-dimensional ST data often have limited spatial resolution and exhibit considerable noise and sparsity, posing significant challenges in deciphering subtle spatial structures and underlying biological activities. Here, we introduce SpaHDmap, an interpretable dimension reduction framework that enhances spatial resolution by integrating ST gene expression with high-resolution histology images. SpaHDmap incorporates non-negative matrix factorization into a multimodal fusion encoder-decoder architecture, enabling the identification of interpretable, high-resolution embeddings. Furthermore, SpaHDmap can simultaneously analyze multiple samples and is compatible with various types of histology images. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real ST datasets from various technologies and tissue types demonstrate that SpaHDmap can effectively produce highly interpretable, high-resolution embeddings, and detects refined spatial structures. SpaHDmap represents a powerful approach for integrating ST data and histology images, offering deeper insights into complex tissue structures and functions.

Spatially resolved omics (SRO) technologies enable the identification of cell types while preserving their organization within tissues. Application of such technologies offers the opportunity to delineate cell-type spatial relationships, particularly across different length scales, and enhance our understanding of tissue organization and function. To quantify such multi-scale cell-type spatial relationships, we developed CRAWDAD, Cell-type Relationship Analysis Workflow Done Across Distances, as an open-source R package with source code and additional documentation at https://jef.works/CRAWDAD/.

To demonstrate the utility of such multi-scale characterization, recapitulate expected cell-type spatial relationships, and evaluate against other cell-type spatial analyses, we applied CRAWDAD to various simulated and real SRO datasets of diverse tissues assayed by diverse SRO technologies. We further demonstrate how such multi-scale characterization enabled by CRAWDAD can be used to compare cell-type spatial relationships across multiple samples. Finally, we applied CRAWDAD to SRO datasets of the human spleen to identify consistent as well as patient and sample-specific cell-type spatial relationships. In general, we anticipate such multi-scale analysis of SRO data enabled by CRAWDAD will provide useful quantitative metrics to facilitate the identification, characterization, and comparison of cell-type spatial relationships across axes of interest.

We report a cellular barcoding strategy, SpaceBar, that enables simultaneous clone tracing and spatial transcriptomics profiling. Our approach uses a library of 96 synthetic barcode sequences that can be robustly detected by imaging based spatial transcriptomics (seqFISH), delivered such that each cell is labeled with a combination of barcodes. We used these barcodes to label melanoma cells in a tumor xenograft model and profiled both clone identity and spatial gene expression in situ. We developed a gene scoring metric that quantifies how strongly gene expression is driven by intrinsic cellular cues or extrinsic environmental signals. Our framework distinguishes between clonal dynamics and environmentally-driven transcriptional regulation in complex tissue contexts.

Spatial transcriptomics is advancing molecular biology by providing high-resolution insights into gene expression within the spatial context of tissues. This context is essential for identifying spatial domains, enabling the understanding of micro-environment organizations and their implications for tissue function and disease progression. To improve current model limitations on multiple slides, we have designed Novae (https://github.com/MICS-Lab/novae), a graph-based foundation model that extracts representations of cells within their spatial contexts. Our model was trained on a large dataset of nearly 30 million cells across 18 tissues, allowing Novae to perform zero-shot domain inference across multiple gene panels, tissues, and technologies. Unlike other models, it also natively corrects batch effects and constructs a nested hierarchy of spatial domains. Furthermore, Novae supports various downstream tasks, including spatially variable gene or pathway analysis and spatial domain trajectory analysis. Overall, Novae provides a robust and versatile tool for advancing spatial transcriptomics and its applications in biomedical research.

Spatially resolved omics enable the discovery of tissue organization of biological or clinical importance. Despite the existence of several methods, performing a rational analysis including multiple algorithms while integrating different conditions such as clinical data is still not trivial. To make such investigations more accessible, we developed mosna, a Python package to analyze spatial omics data with respect to clinical or biological data and to gain insight on cell interaction patterns or tissue architecture of biological relevance. mosna is compatible with all spatial omics methods, it leverages tysserand to build accurate spatial networks, and is compatible with Squidpy. It proposes an analysis pipeline, in which increasingly complex features computed at each step can be explored in integration with clinical data, either with easy-to-use descriptive statistics and data visualization, or by seamlessly training machine learning models and identifying variables with the most predictive power.

mosna can take as input any dataset produced by spatial omics methods, including sub-cellular resolved transcriptomics (MERFISH, seqFISH) and proteomics (CODEX, MIBI-TOF, low-plex immuno-fluorescence), as well as spot-based spatial transcriptomics (10x Visium). Integration with experimental metadata or clinical data is adapted to binary conditions, such as biological treatments or response status of patients, and to survival data. We demonstrate the proposed analysis pipeline on two spatially resolved proteomic datasets containing either binary response to immunotherapy or survival data. mosna identifies features describing cellular composition and spatial distribution that can provide biological insight regarding factors that affect response to immunotherapies or survival.

Availability and implementationmosna is made publicly available to the community, together with relevant documentation and tutorials implemented as Jupyter notebooks to reproduce the result at https://github.com/AlexCoul/mosna

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has transformed our understanding of tissue architecture and cellular interactions, but integrating ST data across platforms remains challenging due to differences in gene panels, data sparsity, and technical variability. Here, we introduce LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW, a novel framework for integrating imaging-based ST data from diverse platforms without requiring shared gene panels. LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW addresses ST integration through two key alignment tasks: feature alignment across technologies and batch alignment across datasets. Optimal transport-guided feature propagation adjusts data sparsity to match scRNA-seq references through graph-based imputation, enabling single-cell foundation models such as scGPT to generate unified features. Batch alignment then refines scGPT-transformed embeddings, mitigating batch effects while preserving biological variability. Evaluations on mouse brain samples from five different technologies demonstrate that LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW outperforms existing methods and is effective for cross-technology spatial gene program identification and tissue slice alignment. Applying LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW to five ovarian cancer datasets, we identify an integrated gene program indicative of tumor-infiltrating T cells across gene panels. Together, LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW provides a robust foundation for cross-platform ST studies, with the potential to scale to large atlas datasets, enabling deeper insights into cellular organization and tissue environments.

Diagnosis and prognosis of neurodegeneration is challenging. This task is important for several neurological disease diagnostic and prognosis, being them designed for patients diagnosed, who often have accumulated genetic damage. Here we propose and evaluate an alternative approach using pretrained computer vision models for decoding automated deep patient images. Deep brain lesion classification based on neurons, is a state of the art in neurological image dataset, as documented in other publications. Interestingly, we found that computer vision models from trained on single animal domain images often do not generalize well to datasets from different animals, such as mouse and humans. Our current best performing model, DeepMind, scored 82% in mouse lesion classification, while the unseen human-derived model did not compare well. Importantly, we found that for human pathology detection, model performance is strongly impacted by the fact whether the image has been submitted to openly available datasets or not. We create robust fusion models based on independently labeled images, and show the combined model can reach model AUC of 94% in mouse lesion classification and 90% in human pathology detection. Here we demonstrate that deep image analysis of computer vision models performed poorly with human image data, compared to mouse-based data, which is potentially rooted in uneven distribution of accessible machine learning datasets and/or unevenly supervised training datasets of computer vision models. These findings are backed by high-dimensional feature values extracted by the model. Our fully automatic lesion detection deep network based on self-supervised pre-trained model, Z-SN-DNN, is envisioned as a step towards a multi-approach approach to characterize deep brain lesion in different species and organs.
